ENCODING · WORKED GUIDE

Invalid Base64: why decoding fails

First identify the input format, then validate the encoding, then interpret the decoded bytes. A padding error, an alphabet mismatch and a UTF-8 failure happen at different stages and need different checks.

By ParseCove · Published 27 November 2026

On this pageWhere to startTry complete examplesPadding and trailing bitsJavaScript & PythonInterpret the bytesTerms & FAQ

Check the wrapper, alphabet and output type

  1. Identify what you copied. A raw Base64 value, a data URL, a JSON field and a complete dot-separated token are different input forms. Parse the surrounding format before passing its encoded value to a decoder.
  2. Choose the expected alphabet. Standard Base64 uses + and /; Base64URL uses the ASCII hyphen - and underscore _. Use the field’s documented format.
  3. Validate before interpreting bytes. Check the characters, length, explicit padding and canonical trailing bits. Only then ask whether the decoded bytes are UTF-8 text, an image or another format.

The tools and snippets here intentionally ignore whitespace and reject other unexpected characters. Decoders in other environments may apply different policies. A successful format check also does not prove that a value is complete, authentic or the data type you expected.

DECODED BYTES · HEX

The explicit padded value has three characters, so its padding is incomplete. This checker accepts Zg or Zg==, but it does not treat Zg= as either form.

See the same padding error in the text decoder

Missing padding and incorrect padding are different

Zg== is a padded encoding of the UTF-8 character f. This checker also accepts the unpadded Zg. It rejects Zg=, because the explicitly padded value has an invalid length. Whether unpadded values are permitted is part of the receiving format’s contract.

CheckWhat it tells you
Payload length modulo 4 is 1The value cannot represent a complete final Base64 group.
Padding appears in the middleThe supplied representation is malformed.
Unused final bits are non-zeroA strict canonical check can reject a value that a permissive decoder accepts.
All format checks passYou have a valid representation of some bytes, not proof that the original data was complete or correct.

For a concrete trailing-bit example, a permissive decoder may turn Zh== into f. Re-encoding that byte gives Zg==, revealing the non-canonical spelling. This site rejects it. For unknown input, check the source rather than guessing replacement characters.

Reference: RFC 4648, sections 3.2–3.5: padding, alphabets and canonical encoding.

Separate byte validation from UTF-8 decoding in code

These complete examples use the standard alphabet and accept valid unpadded values. They deliberately cap small examples at 4,096 encoded characters after whitespace removal. The two tools have their own documented size limits.

JavaScript: validate bytes, then decode UTF-8

function readStandardBase64(value) {
  const clean = value.replace(/\s/g, '');
  if (clean.length > 4096) throw new Error('Small-example limit.');
  if (!/^[A-Za-z0-9+/]*={0,2}$/.test(clean)) throw new Error('Alphabet.');
  const bare = clean.replace(/=+$/, '');
  if (bare.length % 4 === 1 || (clean.includes('=') && clean.length % 4 !== 0)) {
    throw new Error('Length or padding.');
  }
  const binary = atob(bare + '='.repeat((4 - bare.length % 4) % 4));
  if (btoa(binary).replace(/=+$/, '') !== bare) throw new Error('Trailing bits.');
  return Uint8Array.from(binary, char => char.charCodeAt(0));
}
for (const sample of ['Zg==', 'Zg', 'Zg=', 'a$bc', 'Zh==', '+//v', '8J-YgA']) {
  try {
    const bytes = readStandardBase64(sample);
    let result;
    try { result = new TextDecoder('utf-8', { fatal: true }).decode(bytes); }
    catch { result = 'valid bytes; not UTF-8 text'; }
    console.log(sample + ': ' + result);
  } catch { console.log(sample + ': rejected'); }
}

The browser’s atob() returns a binary string. The byte check above re-encodes that result to check canonical trailing bits; TextDecoder with fatal: true then reports malformed UTF-8 instead of silently inserting replacement characters.

Python 3: the same checks and complete sample loop

import base64
import re

def read_standard_base64(value):
    clean = "".join(value.split())
    if len(clean) > 4096:
        raise ValueError("Small-example limit.")
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9+/]*={0,2}", clean):
        raise ValueError("Alphabet.")
    bare = clean.rstrip("=")
    if len(bare) % 4 == 1 or ("=" in clean and len(clean) % 4 != 0):
        raise ValueError("Length or padding.")
    data = base64.b64decode(bare + "=" * (-len(bare) % 4), validate=True)
    if base64.b64encode(data).decode("ascii").rstrip("=") != bare:
        raise ValueError("Trailing bits.")
    return data

for sample in ["Zg==", "Zg", "Zg=", "a$bc", "Zh==", "+//v", "8J-YgA"]:
    try:
        data = read_standard_base64(sample)
        try:
            result = data.decode("utf-8")
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            result = "valid bytes; not UTF-8 text"
        print(sample + ": " + result)
    except ValueError:
        print(sample + ": rejected")

Python’s validate=True rejects non-alphabet characters. The explicit length and re-encoding checks keep this example’s policy consistent for padded and unpadded values. Decode to text only when UTF-8 is the expected content encoding.

References: MDN: atob · MDN: fatal UTF-8 decoding · Python: b64decode.

Valid bytes may need a different tool

Expected contentNext step
UTF-8 text in standard Base64Use Base64 encode / decode.
URL-safe encoded text or binary bytesSelect the matching alphabet or inspect hex in the Base64URL tool.
A HEX byte stringUse the HEX to text decoder and inspect its bytes separately from UTF-8 text.
A PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP imageUse Base64 to image to check the signature, preview and original-byte download.
A full image data URLUse the image viewer’s data URL input. The image-saving guide explains its prefix and payload.
A dot-separated tokenIdentify the encoded segment and its documented alphabet. Decoding a segment does not verify a token’s signature or claims.

The binary example in the walkthrough contains fb ff ef. It is valid Base64 data, but invalid UTF-8 and not a supported image signature. Binary data can also represent compressed files or text in a different character encoding. Identify the original format instead of forcing it through a text decoder.

Terms used in this guide

Alphabet
The permitted encoding symbols. Standard and URL-safe Base64 differ in their last two symbols.
Padding
Trailing = characters used by padded Base64 representations to complete their final group.
Canonical encoding
A normalized encoding of the bytes, including zero values in the unused trailing bits.
UTF-8 validation
A separate check that a byte sequence represents valid UTF-8 text. Passing Base64 validation does not establish that.

Common questions

Is a value without = always invalid?

No. Some formats allow unpadded Base64 or Base64URL. Check the length, trailing bits and receiving protocol rather than treating missing padding as proof of corruption.

Should I strip every non-alphanumeric character?

No. Characters such as +, /, -, _ and = may be meaningful. Parse wrappers deliberately, select the correct alphabet and get the original value if unexpected characters remain.

Does unreadable decoded text mean Base64 is broken?

Not necessarily. The encoded bytes may be binary data or text in another character encoding. Check the expected content type and inspect bytes before choosing a text decoder.

Can I repair a truncated value by adding padding?

Padding cannot recover missing data. It can complete a valid unpadded representation, but a truncated payload may remain wrong even if a decoder accepts its syntax.
